The principal commercial terms of the Placement Agent Agreement are expected to include the following:
154: 
155: > \(a\) Placement fee of 1.50% of committed capital sourced by sagebrush from third-party investors;
156: >
157: > \(b\) 100% offset of placement fees against the management fee payable by the Fund, such that placement fees are economically borne by the general partner and the management company rather than the limited partners;
158: >
159: > \(c\) A retainer of \$150,000, payable upon execution of the Placement Agent Agreement, to be credited against earned placement fees;
160: >
161: > \(d\) A tail period of 24 months following the termination of the Placement Agent Agreement, during which sagebrush will be entitled to placement fees on commitments received from investors introduced by sagebrush during the term of the engagement.
162:

The target execution date for the Placement Agent Agreement is **July 15, 2026**. The Placement Agent Agreement will be governed by the laws of the State of New York.
164:

166: 
167: Calderwood & Harkness will prepare a Side Letter Framework Memorandum (the \"Side Letter Memo\") analyzing standard concessions and investor-specific terms that the Client may expect to negotiate with anticipated anchor investors and other significant limited partners. 169: > \(a\) Fee discounts and co-investment rights;
170: >
171: > \(b\) Most favored nation (\"MFN\") mechanics, including the scope of MFN elections, carve-outs for certain investor-specific provisions, and the procedures for MFN notification and election;
172: >
173: > \(c\) Reporting and transparency requirements;
174: >
175: > \(d\) Key person and LPAC participation;
176: >
177: > \(e\) Excuse and exclusion rights;
178: >
179: > \(f\) Transfer and secondary market provisions; and
180: >
181: > \(g\) Regulatory, tax, and ERISA-specific accommodations.

183: As investor commitments are received and side letter negotiations are initiated, Calderwood & Harkness will draft, negotiate, and finalize individual side letters on behalf of the Client.

189: > \(a\) **SEC Form D Filing.** Preparation and filing of SEC Form D in connection with the offering of limited partnership interests in the Fund under Regulation D of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, under either Rule 506(b) or Rule 506(c), as determined in consultation with the Client;
190: >
191: > \(b\) **Blue Sky Filings.** Preparation and filing of state securities notice filings (blue sky filings) in each jurisdiction in which limited partnership interests are offered or sold, as required;
192: >
193: > \(c\) **Form ADV Amendment / Registration Evaluation.** Amendment of Cobalt\'s existing Form ADV filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the Fund launch. We understand that Cobalt currently maintains Exempt Reporting Adviser status under SEC File No. 802-11934. Calderwood & Harkness, in coordination with Fielding & O\'Hara PLLC (Brian Liddell, Partner), the Client\'s regulatory counsel for SEC investment adviser compliance, Advisers Act exemptions, and Form ADV matters, will evaluate whether the launch of CLSO Fund I and the anticipated increase in regulatory assets under management will require Cobalt to transition from Exempt Reporting Adviser status to full registration as an investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940;
194: >
195: > \(d\) **ERISA/VCOC Compliance.** Monitoring and advising on compliance with ERISA plan asset rules, including the maintenance of VCOC status as described in Section 3.3(a) above;
196: >
197: > \(e\) **OFAC/AML/KYC Requirements.** Advising on the anti-money laundering, know-your-customer, and OFAC screening procedures to be implemented in connection with the acceptance of investor subscriptions; and
198: >
199: > \(f\) **State-Specific Notice Filings.** Preparation of any additional state-specific notice filings required in connection with the Fund\'s activities.
200: 
201: Calderwood & Harkness will coordinate with Fielding & O\'Hara PLLC on all matters relating to SEC investment adviser registration, Advisers Act compliance, and Form ADV filings, as Fielding & O\'Hara serves as the Client\'s primary regulatory counsel for those matters.
202: 
203: **3.8 Service Provider Agreements**
204: 
205: Calderwood & Harkness will review and, where requested, negotiate the terms of agreements between the Fund Entities and third-party service providers, including the following:
206: 
207: > \(a\) **Fund Administrator.** Review and negotiation of the fund administration agreement with Halcyon Fund Services, Inc. (Thomas Varga, Director), which will serve as the Fund\'s third-party fund administrator, providing NAV calculation, investor reporting, capital call and distribution processing, and related services;
208: >
209: > \(b\) **Independent Auditor.** Review and negotiation of the engagement letter with Whitfield & Pratt LLP (Maria Sandoval, Partner), which will serve as the Fund\'s independent auditor and will be responsible for the annual audit of the Fund\'s financial statements;
210: >
211: > \(c\) **Insurance.** Review and negotiation of the directors\' and officers\' liability and errors and omissions insurance policies to be procured through Vantage Risk Advisors, Inc. (Laura Benton), including analysis of coverage terms, limits, and exclusions relevant to the Fund\'s investment activities; and
212: >
213: > \(d\) **Custodian and Banking.** Review and negotiation of the custodial and banking agreements with Ridgeway National Bank, N.A. (Steven Cho, Vice President -- Fund Banking), including the terms of the Fund\'s operating accounts, capital call facility (if applicable), and custodial arrangements.
214: 
215: **3.9 Closing Coordination**
216: 
217: Calderwood & Harkness will manage the closing process for the Fund, including the following:
218:

> \(a\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP** --- a Delaware limited partnership, to be formed, which will serve as the main investment vehicle for the Fund;
> \(b\) **Cobalt Life Sciences GP I, LLC** --- a Delaware limited liability company, to be formed, which will serve as the general partner of the Fund;

> \(c\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Management I, LLC** --- a Delaware limited liability company, to be formed, which will serve as the management company and will be party to the management agreement with the Fund; and

> \(d\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I (Blocker), Inc.** --- a Delaware C-Corporation, to be formed if and when determined to be necessary or advisable for purposes of establishing a taxable blocker structure for certain categories of investors, including tax-exempt and non-U.S. limited partners.

The foregoing entities are collectively referred to herein as the \"Fund Entities.\" As formation documents are prepared and filed for each Fund Entity, such entity shall be deemed a client of the Firm under the terms of this Letter without the need for a separate engagement letter, unless the Firm and the Client agree otherwise in writing.

**Important Clarification Regarding Scope of Representation.** Calderwood & Harkness does not represent, and will not represent in connection with this engagement, any individual limited partner or prospective limited partner of the Fund, any placement agent engaged by the Fund (including sagebrush Capital Partners LLC), or any other third-party service provider to the Fund. Each such party should retain and rely upon its own independent legal counsel with respect to its interests in or obligations to the Fund.
**[3. Scope of Engagement]{.underline}**

The scope of Calderwood & Harkness\'s engagement encompasses the following workstreams, each of which is described in greater detail below. To the extent the Client requests legal services that fall outside the scope described in this Section 3, such services will be provided only upon mutual written agreement and may be subject to a separate engagement letter or an amendment to this Letter.
**3.1 Fund Structuring and Entity Formation**

Calderwood & Harkness will advise the Client on the optimal legal and organizational structure for the Fund and will be responsible for the formation of each Fund Entity. This workstream will include the following:

> \(a\) **Structural Analysis.** Analysis of fund structure alternatives, including a single-tier Delaware limited partnership, parallel fund structures (including for non-U.S. investors or investors requiring a separately managed account), blocker corporation arrangements, alternative investment vehicle (\"AIV\") structures, and master-feeder options. Our analysis will take into account the anticipated investor base, the Client\'s investment strategy, tax efficiency, regulatory considerations, and administrative complexity.

> \(b\) **Fund Structuring Memorandum.** Preparation and delivery of a comprehensive Fund Structuring Memorandum setting forth Calderwood & Harkness\'s analysis and recommendations regarding the recommended fund architecture, including a diagram of the proposed entity structure, a summary of the principal advantages and disadvantages of each structural alternative considered, and our recommended approach. The target delivery date for the Fund Structuring Memorandum is **April 30, 2026**.

> \(c\) **Delaware Formation Filings.** Preparation and filing of the Certificate of Limited Partnership for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP, and the Certificates of Formation for Cobalt Life Sciences GP I, LLC and Cobalt Life Sciences Management I, LLC, with the Delaware Division of Corporations. If the blocker corporation is determined to be necessary, Calderwood & Harkness will also prepare and file the Certificate of Incorporation for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I (Blocker), Inc.
> \(d\) **EIN Applications.** Preparation and submission of IRS Form SS-4 (Application for Employer Identification Number) for CLSO Fund I, CLSO GP I, and CLSO Management I.

> \(e\) **Registered Agent Coordination.** Coordination with Hollowell Technologies, the Client\'s designated registered agent in Delaware, to ensure that each Fund Entity is properly set up for service of process and annual compliance filings.
**3.2 Tax Structuring**
Calderwood & Harkness will provide tax structuring advice in connection with the formation and operation of the Fund, including the following:

> \(a\) **Tax Structuring Memorandum.** Preparation and delivery of a Tax Structuring Memorandum addressing the following topics, among others: (i) unrelated business taxable income (\"UBTI\") and effectively connected income (\"ECI\") planning for tax-exempt and non-U.S. investors; (ii) the application of IRC §1061 to carried interest allocations, including holding period analysis and the implications of the three-year holding period requirement; (iii) state income tax nexus considerations for the Fund, the general partner, and the management company, with a particular focus on Delaware, California, Oregon, Connecticut, and Massachusetts; (iv) blocker corporation structuring, including the use of a Delaware C-Corporation to mitigate UBTI and ECI for certain categories of investors; and (v) carry escrow implications, including the tax treatment of amounts held in escrow and the timing of income recognition. The target delivery date for the Tax Structuring Memorandum is **April 30, 2026**.

> \(b\) **Coordination with Tax Advisor.** Calderwood & Harkness will coordinate with Greystone Tax Advisors LLC (Kenneth Liu, Managing Director), the Client\'s independent tax advisor, on all tax structuring matters. We understand that Greystone will be responsible for the preparation of the Fund\'s annual tax returns (Forms 1065 and Schedules K-1) and for providing ongoing tax compliance advice, and that Calderwood & Harkness\'s role is limited to tax structuring and tax-related provisions of the fund documents.
**3.3 Fund Documentation Drafting**
Calderwood & Harkness will prepare the principal fund documents for the Fund, including the following:

> \(a\) **Agreement of Limited Partnership.** Drafting of the Agreement of Limited Partnership of Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP (the \"LPA\"), including all schedules and exhibits thereto. The first draft of the LPA is targeted for delivery on or about **May 31, 2026**. The LPA will address, among other things, the following key economic and governance terms:
> *Economic Terms:*
> • Management Fee: 2.00% per annum of committed capital during the investment period, stepping down to 2.00% of invested capital (or net invested capital, as determined) thereafter;
> • Carried Interest: 20% of net profits, subject to the preferred return and GP catch-up described below;
> • Preferred Return: 8% per annum, compounded annually;
> • GP Catch-up: 100% of distributions after the preferred return has been achieved, until the general partner has received 20% of cumulative net profits;
> • Carry Escrow: 30% of carried interest distributions to be held in escrow pending final liquidation of the Fund to secure the general partner\'s clawback obligation;

> • Clawback: Standard general partner clawback obligation, net of taxes, to be triggered upon final liquidation of the Fund to the extent the general partner has received carried interest distributions in excess of amounts to which it is entitled on a cumulative basis;
> • Recycling Allowance: 15% of aggregate committed capital may be recycled (i.e., proceeds from realized investments may be recalled for reinvestment during the investment period);
> • Concentration Limit: No more than 15% of aggregate committed capital may be invested in any single portfolio company, measured at the time of investment;
> • Organizational Expense Cap: Organizational expenses in excess of \$1,500,000 shall be borne by the general partner or the management company;
> • Broken-Deal Expense Cap: Broken-deal expenses in excess of \$500,000 per unconsummated transaction shall be borne by the general partner or the management company.
> *Governance Provisions:*
> • Key Person Event provisions, identifying Dr. Marcus Yeung and Priya Dasgupta as key persons, with suspension of the investment period upon a key person event and reinstatement mechanics;
> • Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\") provisions, including composition, authority, and procedures for the resolution of conflicts of interest;
> • Removal rights, including removal of the general partner for cause and no-fault removal by a supermajority in interest of the limited partners;
> • Default provisions, including the consequences of a limited partner\'s failure to fund a capital call;
> • Excuse and exclusion provisions, permitting limited partners to be excused or excluded from particular investments under specified circumstances (e.g., legal, regulatory, or tax impediments).
> *Regulatory Provisions:*

> • ERISA compliance provisions, including the Fund\'s election to qualify as a \"venture capital operating company\" (\"VCOC\") under Department of Labor Regulation §2510.3-101(d), and the related covenants and operating requirements necessary to maintain VCOC status.

> \(b\) **GP LLC Agreement.** Drafting of the Limited Liability Company Agreement of Cobalt Life Sciences GP I, LLC (the \"GP LLC Agreement\"), setting forth the rights, obligations, and economic arrangements of the members of the general partner entity.

> \(c\) **Management Company LLC Agreement.** Drafting of the Limited Liability Company Agreement of Cobalt Life Sciences Management I, LLC (the \"Management Company LLC Agreement\"), setting forth the organizational and operational terms of the management company.

> \(d\) **Subscription Agreement and Investor Questionnaire.** Preparation of the form Subscription Agreement and Investor Questionnaire to be executed by each limited partner at the time of its commitment to the Fund, including representations and warranties regarding accredited investor and qualified purchaser status, ERISA status, tax status, OFAC compliance, and beneficial ownership.
**3.4 Private Placement Memorandum**

Calderwood & Harkness will prepare the confidential Private Placement Memorandum (the \"PPM\") for the Fund. The PPM will be the principal marketing and disclosure document used in connection with the offering of limited partnership interests in the Fund to prospective investors. We anticipate delivering an outline and first draft of the PPM on or about **June 30, 2026**. The PPM will include, among other things, the following:
> \(a\) An executive summary of the terms of the offering;
> \(b\) A description of the Fund\'s investment strategy, investment process, and target sectors within the life-sciences space;
> \(c\) A comprehensive discussion of risk factors associated with an investment in the Fund, including market risks, strategy-specific risks, regulatory risks, and structural risks;
> \(d\) Regulatory disclosures, including disclosures required under applicable federal and state securities laws;
> \(e\) Biographies of the principals and key investment professionals of Cobalt;

> \(f\) A summary of the material U.S. federal income tax considerations applicable to an investment in the Fund, including considerations for taxable U.S. investors, tax-exempt U.S. investors, and non-U.S. investors; and
> \(g\) Appendices containing the form of LPA and Subscription Agreement, or summaries thereof.
**3.5 Placement Agent Agreement**

Calderwood & Harkness will negotiate and draft the exclusive global placement agent agreement (the \"Placement Agent Agreement\") between the Client (or the general partner of the Fund, as applicable) and sagebrush Capital Partners LLC (\"Sagebrush\") (CRD No. 298714; primary contact: Jonathan Mercer, Managing Director). We understand that sagebrush will serve as the exclusive global placement agent for the Fund, subject to certain carve-outs for the Client\'s existing investor relationships. The principal commercial terms of the Placement Agent Agreement are expected to include the following:
> \(a\) Placement fee of 1.50% of committed capital sourced by sagebrush from third-party investors;

> \(b\) 100% offset of placement fees against the management fee payable by the Fund, such that placement fees are economically borne by the general partner and the management company rather than the limited partners;
> \(c\) A retainer of \$150,000, payable upon execution of the Placement Agent Agreement, to be credited against earned placement fees;

> \(d\) A tail period of 24 months following the termination of the Placement Agent Agreement, during which sagebrush will be entitled to placement fees on commitments received from investors introduced by sagebrush during the term of the engagement.

Calderwood & Harkness will coordinate with Ashworth & Lyle LLP (Sara Phan, Partner), counsel to sagebrush, in connection with the negotiation and finalization of the Placement Agent Agreement. The target execution date for the Placement Agent Agreement is **July 15, 2026**. The Placement Agent Agreement will be governed by the laws of the State of New York.
**3.6 Side Letter Framework**

Calderwood & Harkness will prepare a Side Letter Framework Memorandum (the \"Side Letter Memo\") analyzing standard concessions and investor-specific terms that the Client may expect to negotiate with anticipated anchor investors and other significant limited partners. The Side Letter Memo will address, among other things, the following:
> \(a\) Fee discounts and co-investment rights;
> \(b\) Most favored nation (\"MFN\") mechanics, including the scope of MFN elections, carve-outs for certain investor-specific provisions, and the procedures for MFN notification and election;
> \(c\) Reporting and transparency requirements;
> \(d\) Key person and LPAC participation;
> \(e\) Excuse and exclusion rights;
> \(f\) Transfer and secondary market provisions; and
> \(g\) Regulatory, tax, and ERISA-specific accommodations.
As investor commitments are received and side letter negotiations are initiated, Calderwood & Harkness will draft, negotiate, and finalize individual side letters on behalf of the Client.
**3.7 Regulatory Compliance**

Calderwood & Harkness will prepare and maintain a comprehensive Regulatory Compliance Checklist to track the Fund\'s compliance obligations throughout the formation and fund-raising process. The Regulatory Compliance Checklist will address, among other things, the following:

> \(a\) **SEC Form D Filing.** Preparation and filing of SEC Form D in connection with the offering of limited partnership interests in the Fund under Regulation D of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, under either Rule 506(b) or Rule 506(c), as determined in consultation with the Client;

> \(b\) **Blue Sky Filings.** Preparation and filing of state securities notice filings (blue sky filings) in each jurisdiction in which limited partnership interests are offered or sold, as required;

> \(c\) **Form ADV Amendment / Registration Evaluation.** Amendment of Cobalt\'s existing Form ADV filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the Fund launch. We understand that Cobalt currently maintains Exempt Reporting Adviser status under SEC File No. 802-11934. Calderwood & Harkness, in coordination with Fielding & O\'Hara PLLC (Brian Liddell, Partner), the Client\'s regulatory counsel for SEC investment adviser compliance, Advisers Act exemptions, and Form ADV matters, will evaluate whether the launch of CLSO Fund I and the anticipated increase in regulatory assets under management will require Cobalt to transition from Exempt Reporting Adviser status to full registration as an investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940;
> \(d\) **ERISA/VCOC Compliance.** Monitoring and advising on compliance with ERISA plan asset rules, including the maintenance of VCOC status as described in Section 3.3(a) above;

> \(e\) **OFAC/AML/KYC Requirements.** Advising on the anti-money laundering, know-your-customer, and OFAC screening procedures to be implemented in connection with the acceptance of investor subscriptions; and
> \(f\) **State-Specific Notice Filings.** Preparation of any additional state-specific notice filings required in connection with the Fund\'s activities.

Calderwood & Harkness will coordinate with Fielding & O\'Hara PLLC on all matters relating to SEC investment adviser registration, Advisers Act compliance, and Form ADV filings, as Fielding & O\'Hara serves as the Client\'s primary regulatory counsel for those matters.
**3.8 Service Provider Agreements**
Calderwood & Harkness will review and, where requested, negotiate the terms of agreements between the Fund Entities and third-party service providers, including the following:

> \(a\) **Fund Administrator.** Review and negotiation of the fund administration agreement with Halcyon Fund Services, Inc. (Thomas Varga, Director), which will serve as the Fund\'s third-party fund administrator, providing NAV calculation, investor reporting, capital call and distribution processing, and related services;

> \(b\) **Independent Auditor.** Review and negotiation of the engagement letter with Whitfield & Pratt LLP (Maria Sandoval, Partner), which will serve as the Fund\'s independent auditor and will be responsible for the annual audit of the Fund\'s financial statements;

> \(c\) **Insurance.** Review and negotiation of the directors\' and officers\' liability and errors and omissions insurance policies to be procured through Vantage Risk Advisors, Inc. (Laura Benton), including analysis of coverage terms, limits, and exclusions relevant to the Fund\'s investment activities; and

> \(d\) **Custodian and Banking.** Review and negotiation of the custodial and banking agreements with Ridgeway National Bank, N.A. (Steven Cho, Vice President -- Fund Banking), including the terms of the Fund\'s operating accounts, capital call facility (if applicable), and custodial arrangements.
**3.9 Closing Coordination**
Calderwood & Harkness will manage the closing process for the Fund, including the following:

> \(a\) Preparation and maintenance of a master Closing Checklist and Entity Formation Tracker, to be shared with the Client and updated on a regular basis throughout the formation and fund-raising process;
> \(b\) Coordination of the execution and delivery of all closing documents, including subscription agreements, side letters, and partnership interest certificates (if applicable);
> \(c\) Capital call coordination and preparation of funds flow documentation in connection with each closing;
> \(d\) The following target dates have been established for the Fund\'s formation and fund-raising timeline:
> • **Marketing Commencement:** August 1, 2026
> • **First Close (Minimum):** November 15, 2026 (minimum committed capital at First Close: \$250,000,000)
> • **Final Close:** May 15, 2027
Calderwood & Harkness will work closely with the Client, the placement agent, the fund administrator, and other advisors to ensure a smooth and efficient closing process.

The following professionals at Calderwood & Harkness will be principally responsible for this engagement:

21: **[I. Executive Summary]{.underline}**
22: 
23: The purpose of this memorandum is to provide Briarwood Family Office LLC (\"BFO\") with a comprehensive review and legal analysis of the Amended and Restated Agreement of Limited Partnership of Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P. (the \"Fund\" or \"Fund IV\"), dated December 20, 2023 (the \"LPA\"), in connection with BFO\'s evaluation of a proposed limited partnership commitment of Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$75,000,000) to Fund IV. This memorandum has been prepared at the request of BFO\'s General Counsel, Sandra M. Whitfield, and is intended to assist BFO\'s investment committee in its evaluation and approval process.
24: 
25: Fund IV is organized as a Delaware limited partnership, filed with the Delaware Secretary of State under Certificate Number LP-2023-08841. The Fund is managed by its general partner, Meridian Peak Capital Partners GP IV LLC (the \"GP\" or the \"General Partner\"), a Delaware limited liability company whose sole member is Meridian Peak Capital Advisors LLC (\"MPCA\"). The LPA is governed by the laws of the State of Delaware, and the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act (\"DRULPA\") applies to the extent not expressly modified by the LPA.
26: 
27: Fund IV\'s stated investment strategy is to pursue value-add and opportunistic investments in North American commercial real estate, real estate operating companies, and asset management platforms. The Fund has established a target fund size of \$1,500,000,000 and a hard cap of \$1,750,000,000. The Fund anticipates holding its first close on or about April 30, 2024, with a final close deadline of October 31, 2024. BFO\'s proposed commitment of \$75,000,000 would represent approximately 5.0% of the target fund size and approximately 4.29% of the hard cap, positioning BFO as a meaningful but not anchor-level investor in the Fund.
28: 
29: MPCA was founded in 2011 by Conrad J. Ellsworth and Priya Narayan, who continue to serve as the firm\'s Co-Founders and Managing Partners. Mr. Ellsworth serves as Chief Executive Officer and Ms. Narayan serves as Chief Investment Officer. Since its founding, MPCA has raised three prior funds --- Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund I, L.P., Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund II, L.P., and Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund III, L.P. (collectively, \"Funds I--III\") --- aggregating approximately \$3.2 billion in committed capital. Fund IV represents a meaningful step-up in target fund size relative to the prior fund vintages, and the GP\'s ability to deploy capital effectively at this increased scale is a consideration that BFO should evaluate as part of its broader investment diligence, which is addressed separately in our concurrent PPM Summary & Risk Assessment Memorandum.
30: 
31: **Overall Assessment.** Following a thorough review of the LPA, it is our view that the agreement is broadly consistent with prevailing market terms for a mid-market real estate private equity fund of this size and strategy. The economic terms --- including a 1.75% management fee on committed capital during the Investment Period, a 20% carried interest above an 8% preferred return, and a European (whole-fund) waterfall --- are within the range we observe across comparable funds in the current market environment. However, several provisions in the LPA warrant attention and, in our recommendation, should be the subject of negotiation through a side letter to the LPA. These provisions relate primarily to (i) the absence of excuse and exclusion rights in the base LPA, (ii) the management fee structure, (iii) co-investment rights, (iv) most favored nation protections, (v) enhanced reporting obligations, (vi) key person provisions, (vii) transfer rights, and (viii) confidentiality carve-outs. Our detailed recommendations on each of these points are summarized at Section XV of this memorandum and discussed in the relevant sections throughout.
32: 
33: This memorandum should be read in conjunction with the separate PPM Summary & Risk Assessment Memorandum prepared by Calderwood & Harkness and delivered concurrently to BFO, which addresses the investment risk factors, market positioning, and track record analysis for Fund IV based on the Private Placement Memorandum dated December 15, 2023.
34: 
35: **[II. Defined Terms and Interpretive Provisions]{.underline}**
36: 
37: Throughout this memorandum, we use capitalized terms as defined in the LPA unless otherwise noted. For the convenience of BFO\'s review, we highlight below the key defined terms in the LPA that are most relevant to BFO\'s evaluation of the proposed commitment and that recur throughout this memorandum:
38: 
39: > • **\"Capital Commitment\"** means the total amount that a Limited Partner has committed to contribute to the Fund as set forth in such Limited Partner\'s Subscription Agreement. BFO\'s proposed Capital Commitment is \$75,000,000.
40: >
41: > • **\"Capital Account\"** means, with respect to each Partner, such Partner\'s capital account as maintained by the Fund in accordance with Treasury Regulation Section 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv) and the applicable provisions of the LPA.
42: >
43: > • **\"Carried Interest\"** means the performance-based allocation payable to the General Partner equal to 20% of the Fund\'s net profits in excess of the Preferred Return, as more fully described in Section V.C below.
44: >
45: > • **\"Commitment Period\"** (synonymous with \"Investment Period\") means the period beginning on the date of the Final Close and ending on the fourth anniversary thereof, during which the General Partner may make new Investments on behalf of the Fund. The Commitment Period is subject to early termination upon a Key Person Event as described in Section VIII.
46: >
47: > • **\"Fund Expenses\"** means the operating expenses of the Fund as described in Section 5.4 of the LPA, including audit fees, legal fees, administration fees, valuation expenses, insurance premiums, taxes, regulatory filing costs, broken-deal costs, and other customary expenses of the Fund. Fund Expenses are discussed in detail in Section V.D of this memorandum.
48: >
49: > • **\"Investment\"** means any investment made by the Fund in a Portfolio Company or other asset in furtherance of the Fund\'s investment strategy, including equity investments, debt investments, mezzanine investments, and joint venture interests.
50: >
51: > • **\"Net Asset Value\" or \"NAV\"** means the fair market value of the Fund\'s assets less the Fund\'s liabilities, as determined by the General Partner in accordance with the valuation provisions of the LPA (Section 9.3 of the LPA).
52: >
53: > • **\"Organizational Expenses\"** means the costs and expenses incurred in connection with the formation and organization of the Fund, including legal fees, regulatory filing fees, and printing costs, which are borne by the Fund subject to the cap described in Section V.D of this memorandum.
54: >
55: > • **\"Preferred Return\"** means the annual compounded preferred return of 8% per annum on contributed capital, as described in the waterfall provisions of the LPA.
56: >
57: > • **\"Subscription Agreement\"** means the subscription agreement entered into between the Fund and each Limited Partner in connection with such Limited Partner\'s admission to the Fund.
58: 
59: The LPA specifies that it is governed by, and to be construed in accordance with, the laws of the State of Delaware without regard to conflicts of law principles. The Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act (\"DRULPA\"), 6 Del. C. §§ 17-101 et seq., governs the Fund to the extent not expressly modified by the LPA. The LPA contains extensive interpretation clauses stating that, where the provisions of the LPA expressly address a subject also addressed by DRULPA, the LPA provisions are intended to supersede the default DRULPA provisions. This is standard practice in Delaware limited partnership agreements and permits the parties to contract around certain default provisions of DRULPA (as DRULPA expressly permits), including provisions governing distributions, voting, and dissolution.
60: 
61: The LPA makes reference to the Private Placement Memorandum dated December 15, 2023, which sets forth the Fund\'s offering terms, risk factors, and investment strategy in greater detail. Additionally, we note that the GP filed a Form D with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on January 2, 2024, reflecting the Fund\'s reliance on the private placement exemption under Regulation D of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended. The PPM and Form D are addressed in our separate PPM Summary & Risk Assessment Memorandum.
62: 
63: **[III. Formation, Term, and Fund Structure]{.underline}**
64: 
65: **A. Formation and Structure**
66: 
67: Fund IV was formed as a Delaware limited partnership pursuant to a Certificate of Limited Partnership filed with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware under Certificate Number LP-2023-08841. The Fund\'s organizational structure is consistent with the standard structure employed by institutional real estate private equity funds and provides for a single general partner entity and multiple limited partners admitted through a private placement process.
68: 
69: The General Partner of the Fund is Meridian Peak Capital Partners GP IV LLC, a Delaware limited liability company formed for the sole purpose of serving as the general partner of Fund IV. The sole member of the GP is Meridian Peak Capital Advisors LLC (\"MPCA\"), the MPCA management company entity through which Messrs. Ellsworth and Narayan and the broader MPCA investment team operate. This single-layer GP structure --- in which the GP is a direct subsidiary of the management company --- is standard for funds of this type and does not raise any structural concerns from BFO\'s perspective. We note, however, that because the GP is a limited liability company with a single member, BFO should be aware that any change in control of MPCA (whether through admission of new members, transfer of membership interests, or otherwise) would effectively constitute a change of control of the GP. The LPA does not contain an express change-of-control provision with respect to MPCA, though the Key Person provisions (discussed in Section VIII below) provide some protection against departure of the principal investment professionals.
70: 
71: The Fund\'s registered agent in the State of Delaware is Beacon Statutory Services LLC, located at 1013 Centre Road, Wilmington, Delaware 19805. The General Partner\'s registered agent is also Beacon Statutory Services LLC at the same address. This is a standard commercial registered agent arrangement.
72: 
73: The GP maintains its principal office at 200 Clarendon Street, 42nd Floor, Boston, Massachusetts 02116, which is the primary business address of MPCA and the location from which Fund IV\'s investment activities are expected to be conducted.
74: 
75: The LPA identifies the following key service providers to the Fund:
76: 
77: > • **Fund Administrator:** Granite Ledger Fund Services LLC, located at 100 Summer Street, Suite 2700, Boston, Massachusetts 02110. The client relationship manager for Fund IV at Granite Ledger is Catherine J. Halloran. The fund administrator will be responsible for maintaining the Fund\'s books and records, processing capital calls and distributions, preparing quarterly financial statements, and coordinating with the Fund\'s auditor on annual audited financial statements. Granite Ledger is a well-established fund services provider with a significant presence in the real estate fund administration space.
78: >
79: > • **Fund Auditor:** Brockton Marsh & Associates LLP, located at 500 Boylston Street, 30th Floor, Boston, Massachusetts 02116. The engagement partner for Fund IV at Brockton Marsh is Neil A. Strickland. Brockton Marsh will be responsible for conducting the annual audit of the Fund\'s financial statements. While Brockton Marsh is a reputable regional audit firm, it is not among the Big Four accounting firms. BFO should assess whether the audit quality and market reputation of Brockton Marsh are consistent with BFO\'s expectations for a fund of this size, though we do not consider this to be a material concern from a legal perspective.
80: >
81: > • **Placement Agent:** Pinnacle Capital Markets LLC, located at 399 Park Avenue, 18th Floor, New York, New York 10022. The managing director responsible for the Fund IV placement is Roland S. Abernathy. Pinnacle was engaged by the GP pursuant to a placement agent engagement letter dated November 1, 2023. The placement agent\'s compensation and the offset provisions applicable to BFO are discussed in Section V.B of this memorandum.
82: >
83: > • **GP Counsel:** Ashford Crane & Hewitt LLP, located at 1 Federal Street, Suite 3600, Boston, Massachusetts 02110. Ashford Crane serves as outside legal counsel to the General Partner and MPCA in connection with the formation, offering, and operation of Fund IV. We have been in communication with Harrison K. Drummond and Elaine C. Woodbury of Ashford Crane in connection with BFO\'s diligence process, and we anticipate that any side-letter negotiations will be conducted with Ashford Crane on behalf of the GP.
84: 
85: **B. Fund Term**
86: 
87: The LPA establishes a Fund term of ten (10) years commencing on the date of the Final Close. Assuming the Final Close occurs on October 31, 2024 (the stated deadline), the initial term of the Fund would expire on October 31, 2034.
88: 
89: The LPA further provides for two (2) one-year extension periods, each at the sole discretion of the General Partner, which would extend the Fund term to a maximum of twelve (12) years from the Final Close (i.e., potentially through October 31, 2036). Critically, the LPA does not require Limited Partner consent, LPAC approval, or any form of investor vote for either extension period. The GP may exercise each extension unilaterally by providing written notice to the Limited Partners at least 90 days prior to the expiration of the then-current term.
90: 
91: We note that the absence of any LP consent requirement for the extension periods is a less favorable term from BFO\'s perspective. While the first one-year extension at GP discretion is consistent with common market practice, there is an increasing trend in the institutional private equity market to require some form of investor consent for the second extension year --- typically either (i) approval by the Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\"), or (ii) a vote of a majority or super-majority of Limited Partners. The rationale for such a requirement is that a second extension indicates potential difficulty in realizing the Fund\'s remaining portfolio, and LPs should have a voice in determining whether continued management by the GP is in the best interests of the Fund.
92: 
93: **Recommendation:** We recommend that BFO negotiate a side-letter provision requiring LPAC consent or, alternatively, the affirmative vote of Limited Partners holding a super-majority (66⅔% or 75%) of the aggregate Capital Commitments for the exercise of the second one-year extension. If LPAC consent is the mechanism employed, BFO should ensure it has adequate representation on or access to the LPAC, which is discussed further in Section XI.A below.
94: 
95: **C. Closings.** The LPA contemplates multiple closings for the admission of Limited Partners. The anticipated first close is April 30, 2024. The final close deadline is October 31, 2024, which is six (6) months following the anticipated first close. This six-month window between first and final close is standard for a fund of this size and provides the GP with adequate time to complete its fundraising activities.
96: 
97: Between the first close and the final close, the GP may hold one or more subsequent closings at its discretion to admit additional Limited Partners or to accept increased Capital Commitments from existing Limited Partners. The timing and number of subsequent closings are entirely within the GP\'s discretion, and no minimum or maximum number of closings is specified in the LPA.
98: 
99: The LPA includes an interest equalization mechanism for Limited Partners admitted at subsequent closings after the first close. Under this mechanism, subsequent-close LPs are required to contribute their pro rata share of all capital that has previously been called from first-close LPs, together with interest thereon at a rate equal to the Prime Rate plus 2.0% per annum, calculated from the date of each prior capital call through the date of the subsequent-close LP\'s admission. This interest equalization payment is intended to put subsequent-close LPs in the same economic position as if they had been admitted at the first close. The interest equalization payments are distributed to first-close LPs (and any previously-admitted subsequent-close LPs) in proportion to their respective shares of the prior capital calls. This is a standard provision and does not raise any concerns. Given that BFO is likely to be admitted at or near the first close, we do not anticipate significant interest equalization payments by BFO, though this should be confirmed during the subscription process.
100: 
101: **[IV. Capital Commitments and Capital Calls]{.underline}**
102: 
103: **A. Commitment Mechanics**
104: 
105: BFO\'s proposed Capital Commitment to Fund IV is \$75,000,000. The minimum Capital Commitment established in the LPA is \$10,000,000, subject to the GP\'s right to waive such minimum in its sole discretion. BFO\'s proposed commitment is well in excess of the minimum and, as noted above, represents approximately 5.0% of the target fund size and 4.29% of the hard cap.
106: 
107: Capital calls are issued by the General Partner by written notice delivered to each Limited Partner. The LPA requires that capital call notices be delivered no less than ten (10) business days prior to the funding date. Each capital call notice must specify (i) the aggregate amount being called from all Limited Partners, (ii) the individual Limited Partner\'s pro rata share of the capital call, (iii) the purpose of the capital call (i.e., whether for new investments, follow-on investments, Fund Expenses, or reserves), (iv) the funding date, and (v) wire transfer instructions for remittance. We note that the ten-business-day notice period is standard for institutional real estate funds and provides BFO with adequate time to process funding requests internally.
108: 
109: During the Investment Period, the GP may issue capital calls for any purpose related to the Fund\'s operations, including (i) the acquisition of new investments, (ii) follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies or assets, (iii) payment of Fund Expenses, (iv) establishment of reserves as determined by the GP, and (v) repayment of borrowings under any subscription credit facility.
110: 
111: Following the expiration or termination of the Investment Period, the GP\'s authority to issue capital calls is more limited. Post-Investment Period capital calls may be made only for the following purposes: (i) follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies or assets (subject to the 18-month limitation discussed in Section VI.A below), (ii) payment of Fund Expenses, (iii) establishment or maintenance of reserves, and (iv) repayment of borrowings under credit facilities. No capital may be called post-Investment Period for the purpose of making new investments.
112: 
113: The General Partner is required to fund its own GP Capital Commitment on a pari passu basis with the Limited Partners --- that is, the GP must fund its pro rata share of each capital call at the same time and in the same proportion as the Limited Partners. The GP\'s Capital Commitment is established in the LPA at 1.0% of aggregate Capital Commitments. At the target fund size of \$1,500,000,000, the GP\'s anticipated commitment would be \$15,000,000. This 1.0% GP commitment is standard for the market, though we note that some institutional investors prefer a GP commitment in the range of 1.5%--3.0% to ensure stronger alignment of interest between the GP and the LPs. BFO may wish to consider this point in its broader investment evaluation, though we do not recommend it as a side-letter negotiation item as it is unlikely to be modified for a single investor.
114: 
115: **B. Overcall and Recycling Provisions**
116: 
117: **Recycling.** The LPA permits the GP to recycle investment proceeds --- that is, to recall and reinvest capital that has been returned to Limited Partners from realized investments. Recycling is subject to two conditions: (i) the proceeds to be recycled must be derived from investments that were realized within twenty-four (24) months of their initial acquisition, and (ii) the aggregate amount of capital called from Limited Partners (inclusive of recycled capital) may not exceed 125% of total Capital Commitments. This 125% recycling cap means that, in addition to the initial \$75,000,000 Capital Commitment, BFO could potentially be required to fund up to an additional \$18,750,000 in recycled capital calls over the life of the Fund (i.e., \$75,000,000 × 125% = \$93,750,000 total, less \$75,000,000 initial commitment = \$18,750,000 maximum additional recycled calls). We note that the 125% recycling cap is on the higher end of the market range (which typically falls between 110% and 125%) and reflects the GP\'s desire for flexibility in reinvesting early-realization proceeds. While recycling can be beneficial to LPs by increasing the Fund\'s invested capital base and potentially enhancing returns, it also extends the period during which LPs\' capital is subject to call and increases the overall cash outflows from an LP\'s perspective.
118: 
119: **Overcall.** The LPA also contains an overcall provision that permits the GP to call additional capital from non-defaulting Limited Partners in the event that another Limited Partner defaults on a capital call obligation. Under the overcall provision, the GP may call up to 125% of a given non-defaulting LP\'s pro rata share of any capital call to cover a defaulting LP\'s shortfall. This provision creates potential overcall exposure for BFO --- in a default scenario, BFO could be required to fund up to 25% more than its pro rata share of a capital call. The overcall provision is standard in form, though the 125% overcall limit (rather than a lower threshold, such as 110%) is somewhat aggressive.
120: 
121: **Recommendation:** We recommend that BFO monitor both the recycling cap and the overcall provisions carefully. BFO should consider negotiating a side-letter limitation on overcall exposure, potentially capping BFO\'s aggregate overcall obligation at a lower threshold (e.g., 110% of BFO\'s pro rata share of any given capital call, or establishing an absolute dollar cap on aggregate overcall funding over the life of the Fund). We recognize that the GP may resist modifications to the overcall provision, as it serves a structural purpose in protecting the Fund against LP defaults, but the exposure should be flagged for BFO\'s investment committee.
122: 
123: **[V. Fund Economics]{.underline}**
124: 
125: **A. Management Fee**
126: 
127: The management fee structure under the LPA is divided into two tiers based on the Investment Period:
128: 
129: **During the Investment Period (Years 1--4):** The management fee is 1.75% per annum, calculated on the aggregate Capital Commitments of all Limited Partners. For BFO, based on a Capital Commitment of \$75,000,000, the annual management fee during the Investment Period would be:
130: 
131: > \$75,000,000 × 1.75% = \$1,312,500 per year
132: 
133: Over the four-year Investment Period, BFO\'s cumulative management fee burden (absent any negotiated reduction) would be:
134: 
135: > \$1,312,500 × 4 years = \$5,250,000
136: 
137: We note that the management fee during the Investment Period is calculated on committed capital (i.e., the full \$75,000,000), not on called or invested capital. This is standard practice for a fund of this size, but it means that BFO will be paying management fees on the full amount of its commitment from the outset, even though a significant portion of that commitment will remain uncalled during the early years of the Fund\'s life. This represents a real economic cost to BFO, as management fees on uncalled capital effectively reduce the net return on invested capital.
138: 
139: **Post-Investment Period (Years 5--10+):** Following the expiration of the Investment Period, the management fee steps down to 1.50% per annum, calculated on net invested capital (defined as the aggregate cost basis of unrealized investments, less any write-downs approved by the Fund\'s auditor). This post-Investment Period fee structure is favorable to LPs relative to a structure that continues to charge fees on committed capital, as the fee base will decline over time as investments are realized and capital is returned to LPs. The precise amount of the post-Investment Period management fee will vary depending on the pace of portfolio realizations and the extent of any write-downs, and therefore cannot be calculated with certainty at this time.
140: 
141: Management fees are payable quarterly in advance. The GP issues management fee invoices to the Fund (not directly to individual LPs), and management fees are funded through capital calls or, alternatively, through the use of a subscription credit facility, with such fees being allocated among the Limited Partners in proportion to their respective Capital Commitments.
142: 
143: **Proposed Side-Letter Negotiation on Management Fee.** We recommend that BFO negotiate a reduction in the management fee through a side letter, as follows:
144: 
145: > • **Investment Period fee:** Reduce from 1.75% to 1.50% per annum on committed capital (a 25 basis point reduction)
146: >
147: > • **Post-Investment Period fee:** Reduce from 1.50% to 1.25% per annum on net invested capital (a 25 basis point reduction)
148: 
149: The economic impact of the proposed reduction during the Investment Period would be as follows:
150: 
151: > • Negotiated annual fee: \$75,000,000 × 1.50% = \$1,125,000 per year
152: >
153: > • Annual savings: \$1,312,500 − \$1,125,000 = \$187,500 per year
154: >
155: > • Cumulative savings over the four-year Investment Period: \$187,500 × 4 = \$750,000
156: 
157: The post-Investment Period savings would be variable and dependent on the level of net invested capital, but would represent a consistent 25 basis point benefit to BFO throughout the remaining life of the Fund.
158: 
159: We believe a 25 basis point reduction is a reasonable and achievable negotiating objective for a commitment of BFO\'s size. At \$75,000,000, BFO is a meaningful investor representing 5.0% of the target fund size, and fee reductions of this magnitude are commonly granted to investors at or above this commitment level in the current market environment. We anticipate that the GP may counter at a smaller reduction, such as 15 basis points (resulting in rates of 1.60% during the Investment Period and 1.35% post-Investment Period), and we would recommend that BFO be prepared to accept such a counter if it is the GP\'s final position on this point.
160: 
161: **B. Placement Agent Fee Offset**
162: 
163: Pinnacle Capital Markets LLC, the Fund\'s placement agent, is entitled to receive a placement fee equal to 1.0% of the Capital Commitment of each Limited Partner introduced to the Fund through Pinnacle\'s placement activities. Based on BFO\'s proposed Capital Commitment of \$75,000,000, the placement fee attributable to BFO would be:
164: 
165: > \$75,000,000 × 1.0% = \$750,000
166: 
167: The LPA provides that 100% of placement fees incurred with respect to a given Limited Partner are to be offset against the management fees otherwise payable by that Limited Partner. This means that the \$750,000 placement fee attributable to BFO would be credited against BFO\'s management fee obligations, reducing BFO\'s net management fee burden by \$750,000 over the offset period. We have confirmed that this 100% offset provision is contained in the base LPA itself (Section 5.2(d)) and is not limited to investors who have negotiated a specific side-letter provision.
168: 
169: We note, however, that the LPA does not specify the precise mechanics of the placement fee offset --- for example, whether the offset is applied ratably over the Investment Period (i.e., \$750,000 ÷ 4 years = \$187,500 per year), applied in full against the first management fee payment, or applied in some other manner. This ambiguity should be clarified.
170: 
171: **Recommendation:** We recommend that BFO\'s side letter explicitly confirm the 100% offset and specify the timing and mechanics of the offset application. Our preference would be for the offset to be applied as a dollar-for-dollar reduction to the first management fee payments until the \$750,000 offset is fully exhausted, as this would provide the maximum economic benefit to BFO through early recovery of the placement fee amount.
172: 
173: **C. Carried Interest / Performance Allocation**
174: 
175: The General Partner is entitled to a carried interest (referred to in the LPA as the \"Performance Allocation\") equal to 20% of the Fund\'s net profits in excess of the Preferred Return. The carried interest is the primary performance-based compensation mechanism for the GP and its investment professionals.
176: 
177: The carried interest is calculated and distributed in accordance with a whole-fund European-style distribution waterfall, which operates as follows:
178: 
179: **Step 1 --- Return of Contributed Capital.** All distributions are first applied to return to the Limited Partners the aggregate amount of capital contributed by such Limited Partners to the Fund, including capital attributable to recycled investments. This provision ensures that no carried interest is payable to the GP until LPs have received a full return of their invested capital across the entire Fund portfolio.
180: 
181: **Step 2 --- Preferred Return.** After full return of contributed capital, distributions are next applied to pay the Limited Partners a preferred return equal to 8% per annum on contributed capital, compounded annually. The preferred return accrues from the date of each capital contribution and continues to accrue until paid in full. The 8% preferred return is the prevailing market rate for real estate PE funds and is consistent with Funds I--III.
182: 
183: **Step 3 --- GP Catch-Up.** After full payment of the preferred return, the General Partner receives 100% of subsequent distributions until the GP has received an amount equal to 20% of the aggregate profits distributed in Steps 2 and 3 combined. This catch-up mechanism effectively brings the GP\'s cumulative profit share up to 20% of total profits once the preferred return has been satisfied.
184: 
185: **Step 4 --- 80/20 Split.** After completion of the GP catch-up, all remaining distributions are split 80% to the Limited Partners and 20% to the General Partner.
186: 
187: The European (whole-fund) waterfall structure is favorable to BFO and the other Limited Partners relative to a deal-by-deal (American) waterfall structure. In a deal-by-deal waterfall, the GP would be entitled to receive carried interest on profitable investments without first accounting for losses on other investments in the portfolio, creating the risk that the GP receives carried interest on individual deals even if the Fund as a whole has not generated positive returns net of the preferred return. The European waterfall avoids this risk by requiring that carry is calculated and paid only after all contributed capital has been returned and the preferred return has been satisfied across the entire Fund portfolio. This is a meaningful protection for BFO and is consistent with market best practices for real estate PE funds.
188: 
189: We do not recommend any modification to the carried interest terms via side letter. The 20/80 split with an 8% preferred return and European waterfall structure are market-standard, and the GP is unlikely to agree to modifications to these fundamental economic terms for any single LP.
190: 
191: **GP Clawback Obligation.** The LPA includes a GP clawback provision (Section 7.6 of the LPA), which requires the General Partner to return to the Fund, upon liquidation, any carried interest distributions that, in the aggregate, exceed the amount to which the GP would have been entitled based on the final cumulative performance of the Fund. The clawback obligation is secured by an escrow arrangement pursuant to which 25% of all carried interest distributions received by the GP are deposited into a third-party escrow account and held until the earlier of (i) the final liquidation of the Fund or (ii) the date on which the GP can demonstrate that no clawback obligation remains outstanding. The escrow account is maintained by a third-party escrow agent designated by the GP, and the LPA specifies that the escrow funds may be invested in U.S. Treasury obligations or money market funds pending release.
192: 
193: We note that the GP clawback obligation is subject to an after-tax adjustment --- that is, the GP is only required to return the net after-tax amount of any excess carried interest, taking into account the taxes paid or payable by the GP (and its members) on such carried interest distributions. This after-tax clawback adjustment is common in the market but is less favorable to LPs than a gross clawback (which would require the GP to return the full pre-tax amount of excess carry). The practical effect is that LPs bear a portion of the tax cost associated with the GP\'s receipt and subsequent return of excess carry. While we note this point for BFO\'s awareness, we do not recommend attempting to negotiate a gross clawback, as it is unlikely to be accepted by the GP and the after-tax adjustment is the prevailing market standard.
194: 
195: Additionally, the 25% escrow rate is at the lower end of the market range (which typically falls between 25% and 50%). A higher escrow rate would provide greater security for the clawback obligation. BFO may wish to raise the escrow percentage as a negotiating point, though we consider this a lower priority relative to the other items identified in Section XV.
196: 
197: **D. Organizational Expenses and Fund Expenses**
198: 
199: **Organizational Expenses.** The LPA provides that organizational expenses incurred in connection with the formation and structuring of the Fund are borne by the Fund, subject to a cap of \$2,500,000. To the extent that organizational expenses exceed this cap, the excess is borne by the GP and not allocated to the Fund or its Limited Partners. Organizational expenses typically include legal fees incurred in preparing the LPA, PPM, and subscription documents, regulatory filing fees (including SEC and state blue sky filings), accounting fees for initial tax structuring, and printing and distribution costs. The \$2,500,000 cap is within the range we observe for funds of this size (typically \$1,500,000--\$3,000,000) and is acceptable.
200: 
201: **Fund Expenses.** The LPA provides for a broad category of ongoing Fund Expenses that are borne by the Fund (and therefore allocated among the Limited Partners in proportion to their respective Capital Commitments or, after the Investment Period, their respective shares of net invested capital). Fund Expenses include, without limitation:
202: 
203: > \(a\) Audit fees payable to Brockton Marsh & Associates LLP in connection with the annual audit of the Fund\'s financial statements;
204: >
205: > \(b\) Legal fees and expenses incurred by the Fund in connection with its operations, investments, and regulatory compliance (excluding fees incurred by the GP for its own benefit);
206: >
207: > \(c\) Administration fees payable to Granite Ledger Fund Services LLC for fund administration, accounting, and reporting services;
208: >
209: > \(d\) Valuation expenses incurred in connection with the appraisal and valuation of the Fund\'s investments, including fees payable to independent appraisers;
210: >
211: > \(e\) Insurance premiums, including directors\' and officers\' liability insurance, general liability insurance, and errors and omissions coverage;
212: >
213: > \(f\) Taxes, including any entity-level taxes imposed on the Fund (which are generally not expected given the Fund\'s partnership structure for U.S. federal income tax purposes, but which may include state and local taxes in certain jurisdictions);
214: >
215: > \(g\) Regulatory filing costs, including costs of maintaining the Fund\'s qualification and filings under applicable state and federal securities laws;
216: >
217: > \(h\) Broken-deal costs (also referred to as \"abort costs\"), including expenses incurred by the Fund in connection with potential investments that are not consummated, such as due diligence expenses, legal fees, travel costs, environmental assessments, appraisal fees, and any deposit forfeiture amounts; and
218: >
219: > \(i\) Other customary expenses of the Fund, including travel, custody, and other operational costs.
220: 
221: We draw BFO\'s particular attention to the broken-deal costs provision. The LPA allocates broken-deal costs to the Fund without any cap or limitation. In an active investment environment where the GP is pursuing multiple opportunities simultaneously, broken-deal costs can be substantial --- it is not uncommon for a single failed acquisition to generate \$500,000 or more in abort costs (including legal fees, environmental reports, engineering studies, and appraisal fees). Over the life of the Fund, aggregate broken-deal costs could be significant, particularly given Fund IV\'s strategy of pursuing value-add and opportunistic investments in commercial real estate, which often involves competitive auction processes with high due diligence expenses.
222: 
223: **Recommendation:** We recommend that BFO consider requesting a side-letter provision either (i) capping BFO\'s share of broken-deal costs at a specified dollar amount or percentage of BFO\'s Capital Commitment, or (ii) requiring enhanced disclosure of broken-deal costs in the Fund\'s quarterly reporting packages. Of these two approaches, enhanced disclosure is more likely to be accepted by the GP, as an individualized cap on broken-deal costs for a single LP would be difficult to administer. At a minimum, BFO should ensure that the quarterly financial statements provide a line-item breakdown of broken-deal costs incurred during the period, including a brief description of the transactions to which such costs relate.
224: 
225: **[VI. Investment Period and Investment Restrictions]{.underline}**
226: 
227: **A. Investment Period**
228: 
229: The Investment Period (referred to in the LPA as the \"Commitment Period\") commences on the date of the Final Close and continues for a period of four (4) years. Assuming the Final Close occurs on October 31, 2024, the Investment Period would expire on October 31, 2028. During the Investment Period, the GP has broad authority to deploy the Fund\'s capital in new investments in accordance with the Fund\'s investment strategy and subject to the investment restrictions described below.
230: 
231: Upon expiration of the Investment Period, the GP may not make new investments on behalf of the Fund. However, the LPA permits the GP to make follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies or assets for a period of eighteen (18) months following the expiration of the Investment Period (i.e., through April 30, 2030, assuming an Investment Period expiration of October 31, 2028). Follow-on investments are investments in existing portfolio assets that are made for the purpose of preserving or enhancing the value of an existing investment, such as additional equity contributions to fund capital improvements, tenant improvement allowances, or debt service shortfalls. The 18-month follow-on period is consistent with market practice for real estate PE funds.
232: 
233: As discussed in Section VIII below, the Investment Period is subject to early termination upon the occurrence of a Key Person Event that is not cured within the applicable cure period.
234: 
235: **B. Investment Strategy and Restrictions**
236: 
237: The LPA defines the Fund\'s investment strategy as the pursuit of value-add and opportunistic investments in North American commercial real estate, real estate operating companies, and asset management platforms. This is a broad investment mandate that encompasses a wide range of real estate asset types, including office, multifamily, industrial, retail, hospitality, and specialty asset classes, as well as investments in operating platforms that manage or develop real estate assets.
238: 
239: The geographic focus of the Fund is limited to the United States and Canada (collectively, \"North America\"). The LPA does not permit investments outside of North America, which limits the Fund\'s exposure to cross-border and emerging market risks. This geographic limitation is appropriate given MPCA\'s track record and investment expertise, which has been predominantly focused on the U.S. market.
240: 
241: The LPA establishes the following concentration limits on the Fund\'s investment activities:
242: 
243: > \(a\) **Single Investment Concentration:** No single investment may exceed 20% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments. At the target fund size of \$1,500,000,000, this equates to a maximum single investment of approximately \$300,000,000. This concentration limit is standard for a diversified real estate fund and provides reasonable protection against single-asset risk.
244: >
245: > \(b\) **Geographic Concentration:** No more than 30% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments may be invested in any single market or metropolitan statistical area (\"MSA\"). At the target fund size, this equates to a maximum geographic concentration of approximately \$450,000,000 in any single MSA. This limit provides some geographic diversification, though the 30% threshold permits significant concentration in a single market.
246: >
247: > \(c\) **Asset Management Platform Concentration:** No more than 25% of the Fund\'s aggregate Capital Commitments may be invested in asset management platform acquisitions. At the target fund size, this equates to a maximum of approximately \$375,000,000 in platform investments. This limit is appropriate given that platform investments carry different risk characteristics than direct real estate investments, including operational risk, key person dependency, and valuation complexity.
248: 
249: **Leverage Restrictions.** The LPA establishes leverage limits at both the fund and investment level. Fund-level borrowing (exclusive of subscription credit facilities) is limited to a maximum loan-to-value (\"LTV\") ratio of 65% on any individual investment. This is within the standard range for value-add and opportunistic real estate strategies, though it permits a meaningful level of leverage that amplifies both potential returns and potential losses. BFO should be aware that the 65% LTV limit applies on an investment-by-investment basis, not at the fund portfolio level, meaning that the Fund\'s aggregate leverage ratio could exceed 65% if certain investments are leveraged at or near the maximum while others are held with lower or no leverage.
250: 
251: The LPA also permits the GP to enter into subscription credit facilities (also known as capital call facilities or subscription lines of credit) secured by the unfunded Capital Commitments of the Limited Partners. The subscription facility is capped at 25% of aggregate unfunded Capital Commitments, with a maximum outstanding term of 180 days (approximately six months). Subscription facilities are commonly used to bridge the timing gap between investment execution and capital call funding, and they can also be used to fund management fees, organizational expenses, and other Fund Expenses. While subscription facilities provide operational flexibility, BFO should be aware that the use of such facilities can have the effect of enhancing reported IRR by delaying capital calls (thereby reducing the period over which LP capital is deemed invested), even though the total dollar return to LPs is unchanged. BFO should consider requesting additional disclosure regarding the Fund\'s use of subscription facilities in its quarterly reporting.
252: 
253: **Investment Restrictions --- Notable Gaps.** We have identified several categories of investments that are not expressly restricted or addressed in the LPA:
254: 
255: > \(a\) **Cannabis-Related Assets.** The LPA does not contain any restriction on investments in real estate assets that are leased to or used in connection with cannabis cultivation, processing, or distribution operations. While cannabis operations are legal under the laws of certain U.S. states, they remain illegal under federal law (the Controlled Substances Act), and investments in cannabis-related real estate present significant legal, regulatory, reputational, and banking risks.
256: >
257: > \(b\) **Gaming/Casino Properties.** The LPA does not contain any restriction on investments in gaming or casino properties. Such investments may require licensing and regulatory approvals in certain jurisdictions and may present reputational considerations for BFO.
258: >
259: > \(c\) **Sanctioned Jurisdictions.** While the LPA contains standard OFAC compliance representations, it does not expressly restrict investments in jurisdictions subject to U.S. sanctions or involving parties on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals List. Given that the Fund\'s geographic mandate is limited to North America, this is a lower risk, but not zero risk.
260: >
261: > \(d\) **ERISA Plan Assets.** The LPA does not contain an express restriction on investments that would cause the Fund (or a subsidiary thereof) to hold \"plan assets\" within the meaning of ERISA Section 3(42) and the Department of Labor\'s plan asset regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-101. While the Fund-level ERISA structure is addressed separately (see Section XIV.B below), the absence of an investment-level ERISA restriction is notable.
262: 
263: The absence of express restrictions in these categories is significant because the base LPA also does not include a general excuse or exclusion mechanism that would permit BFO to opt out of specific investments (see Section VII below).
264: 
265: **Recommendation:** BFO should negotiate side-letter excuse and exclusion rights covering each of the categories identified above. This is discussed in detail in Section VII below and is identified as a high-priority negotiation item in Section XV.
266: 
267: **[VII. Excuse and Exclusion Rights]{.underline}**
268: 
269: **A. LPA Baseline**
270: 
271: The base LPA does **not** include a general excuse or exclusion right for Limited Partners. This is a significant gap in the LPA from BFO\'s perspective. In the absence of an excuse right, BFO would be obligated to fund its pro rata share of every capital call issued by the GP during the Investment Period, regardless of the nature of the underlying investment and regardless of any legal, regulatory, or reputational concerns that BFO may have with respect to such investment.
272: 
273: The LPA provides only a narrow regulatory excuse mechanism in Section 4.5, which states that a Limited Partner may be excused from participation in a specific investment if, in the General Partner\'s reasonable determination, such participation would cause the Limited Partner to violate any applicable law or governmental regulation. This provision places the determination of whether a legal or regulatory conflict exists in the hands of the GP, not the affected LP. There is no investor-initiated excuse mechanism, and the GP retains sole discretion over whether to grant an excuse under this narrow provision.
274: 
275: Furthermore, the LPA does not contain any cap on the aggregate amount of investments from which an LP may be excused, because the general excuse right does not exist in the base document. The narrow regulatory excuse in Section 4.5 is treated as an exception to the mandatory capital call provisions rather than as an affirmative LP right.
276: 
277: The absence of a general excuse right is below market standard for institutional real estate PE funds of this size. In our experience, the majority of fund LPAs in the current market environment include some form of excuse or exclusion mechanism, even if it is limited to specified categories of investments and subject to a cap on the aggregate amount of excused investments.
278: 
279: **B. Side-Letter Recommendation**
280: 
281: We strongly recommend that BFO negotiate an affirmative excuse right through its side letter. The proposed excuse right should be structured as follows:
282: 
283: **Trigger and Notice Mechanism.** Upon receipt of a capital call notice from the GP identifying a proposed investment, BFO would have the right to provide written notice to the GP within fifteen (15) business days exercising its excuse right with respect to such investment. BFO would be required to specify the category of excuse being invoked (from the categories listed below) and to provide a brief description of the basis for BFO\'s determination that the investment falls within the applicable category. The GP would be obligated to honor BFO\'s excuse election without further inquiry, provided that the investment falls within one of the specified categories.
284: 
285: **Categories for Excuse.** We recommend that BFO seek excuse rights with respect to the following categories of investments:
